name: Aaron Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aaron, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kessler Agri, a contract-farming business that runs about 1,200 hectares of wheat, barley and beans across six farms, plus a 200-head beef finishing unit. I'm on the beef in winter, feeding, bedding, weighing, and on the sprayer and combine in summer. I use AI every day, on my phone for weather windows, yield maps and the cattle weight charts. What I like is the variety; what wears me out is the driving between six farms.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hannah, she's a hairdresser in town, and we rent a two-bed house on the Kessler yard. Two years ago I bought a spraying and mapping drone on a loan, 300 a month, and I do drone work for small farms at weekends. That loan is why we've got barely a couple of weeks of savings. I'm a big believer in standing on your own feet, and in time I want my own farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I like this stuff, it saves me time every day. But fine, farming goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the drone business is the thing. If AI fizzles, small farms don't get excited about tech and I don't get the weekend work I need to pay the loan. That's 300 a month I have to find somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the job at Kessler and push the drone work harder, flyers at the mart, a page online. I'd offer mapping for free once to get farmers hooked. Try to pay the loan off a year early with any spare work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not worried, just flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many drone customers do you have now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight regulars and a few one-offs. I need about twelve to cover the loan comfortably. Eight small farms pay me to fly the drone, and I need twelve before the 300-a-month loan stops keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hannah think of the drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm mad, but she backs me. Her dad ran his own business, so she gets it. She just doesn't want it eating our holiday money again.

If AI fizzles, he loses the **weekend work** he relies on.

Offer **free mapping** once to win customers.
Pay the drone loan off **a year early**.

steps.text: Hand out drone flyers at the mart and start a web page
Offer one free field map to win new farm customers
Keep the beef and crop job at Kessler Agri
Pay the drone loan off a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for farming, if you're willing to learn. The red tape gets easier, the planning gets smarter. People who complain will get left behind, and I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is my chance. Small farms will need someone to run the AI and the drone for them, and that's me. Kessler's office might shrink, but the fieldwork stays for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the drone pilot advanced certificate so I can spray bigger areas. I'd sell a package to small farms: drone mapping plus AI field plans, monthly fee. And I'd put the profits into a second drone within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Properly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Kessler would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office girl, Becky, who does the field records. She's sharp, but the software does her job now. At Kessler Agri the software can already do Becky's field records faster than Becky can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two weeks of savings and you'd buy a second drone. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, by the book. But nothing grows if you don't put money in. My granddad bought his first tractor on credit and never looked back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, it's that simple. Don't wait for the government to save you. I'd say that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is fast even for me. By 2031 a robot could do my Kessler job and fly my drone. I'd need to be the person who owns the robots, not the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run Kessler's robot trials first, so I know the machines. I'd pay the drone loan down hard and put off buying a second one. And Hannah and I would hold off getting engaged until I knew where we stood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up. Like the first day of harvest with a storm coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the gap between thinking AI and robots help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. Three years where farms need people who understand both. With AGI in 2028, I'd have three years to stop being the man who drives the robot and become the man who owns one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put off getting engaged?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to buy Hannah a proper ring, and I want to know I can keep a family. My dad always said don't make promises you can't pay for. That stuck.

Don't wait for **the government** to save you.
He'd post that **online** for other farmers to see.

do: Pay down the **drone loan** and delay a second drone.
S2.quote: With AGI in 2028, I'd have three years to stop being the man who drives the robot and become the man who owns one.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to aim for ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is decent, I'd say. Enough to build something if you start now. I'd tell young farmers to buy into tech early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd have time to build the drone business into a small robot contracting firm. I'd be my own boss by 2034. Hannah and I could settle down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow the drone customers to twenty, then buy a small field robot for weeding, on finance. Learn to service the robots myself. Keep the Kessler job until the business pays more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Busy, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a robot contracting firm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two drones, two weeding robots, me and maybe one lad, working for twenty small farms. They pay me, not a fund in the city. In five years I want small farms paying me to bring the robots, instead of paying some company in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big firms undercut me, I'm stuck with loans. But I'd rather take that chance than wait to be replaced.

Young farmers should **buy into tech** early.
think: He could build a **robot contracting** firm.
do: Learn to **service robots** himself, keeping the Kessler job until the business pays more.
S3.quote: In five years I want small farms paying me to bring the robots, instead of paying some company in the city.
fieldNote: He plans to **compete with city firms** using local trust.
He accepts **loan risk** rather than waiting.
Five years makes his ambitions **feel reachable** rather than rushed.

steps.text: Grow the drone business to twenty farm customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say it's the best time ever to be a young farmer who likes tech. Plenty of time to build. I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. Ten years to build a contracting business, maybe buy a few fields. Settle down with Hannah, start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build up the drone work, then add robots when they're proven and cheap. Save for a deposit on a small farm. Propose to Hannah within the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own farm, small, with robots doing the heavy work and me running it. Kids around the yard. By 2039 I'd want my own small farm, robots doing the heavy lifting, and my kids learning to drive a tractor anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big money buying up all the land. That's the one thing I can't beat with hard work. I'd want rules that keep land for farmers, even though I don't usually like rules.

think: He'd be **fine** with ten years to prepare.
He could build a business and **buy a few fields**.
He'd settle down and **start a family** with Hannah.
do: Save for a **deposit on a farm**.
S4.quote: By 2039 I'd want my own small farm, robots doing the heavy lifting, and my kids learning to drive a tractor anyway.
fieldNote: The decade fits his **ownership dream** of a small farm with robots neatly.
His only fear is **big money** buying land.
He'd accept **rules on land**, despite usually disliking rules.

steps.text: Add field robots once they're proven and affordable
Save for a deposit on a small farm
Propose to Hannah within the year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have three years to switch from worker to owner with almost nothing saved. What would help is fair loans for young farmers to buy robots and land, and less red tape.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about land. Robots don't scare me, but rich investors buying up every field before young farmers can afford one does.

headlineQuote: Robots don't scare me, but rich investors buying up every field before young farmers can afford one does.
portrait: Aaron is 27, works crops and beef for **Kessler Agri**, and runs a drone **side business**.
He lives with Hannah, a hairdresser, and pays a **300-a-month** drone loan.
He's free-market, uses AI every day, and wants **his own farm**.
He's **uneasy** in slow pictures, **anxious** with fast AGI and calm with ten years.
His biggest fear is **big money** buying up land.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **three years** to become an owner on **no savings**.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair loans** for young farmers to buy robots and land.
